opus-5.5.text:
You know, one of the things I've learned from building companies at AI Fund is that almost no first-time founder shows up with every skill they need, and honestly, that's fine. I don't think we should expect anyone to be a complete package on day one. What matters much more is whether they can learn quickly and whether they're honest with themselves about where the gaps are.

So the way I think about it is, first, we try to help founders figure out which gaps actually matter for the specific business. If you're building a vertical AI application in, say, healthcare or logistics, maybe the founder has deep domain expertise and really understands the customer, but hasn't yet had to recruit a strong engineering team or think through go-to-market. Those are very different gaps, and they call for different kinds of support.

Second, a lot of it is surrounding them with the right people. Sometimes that means pairing them with a co-founder or an early executive who complements their strengths. Sometimes it means giving them access to a team that's done this many times before, people who can help with things like recruiting, product design, or technical architecture, so the founder doesn't have to reinvent all of that from scratch.

And third, I think there's a lot of value in just giving them repetitions and fast feedback. Much of entrepreneurship is a learnable skill. When a founder makes a decision, sees how it plays out, and gets candid input from someone who's seen that pattern before, they get better remarkably quickly. Speed of iteration really matters, both for the product and for the founder's own growth.

The thing I try not to do is wait until someone has filled every gap before letting them start. If they have the core skills, a deep understanding of a real problem, and the drive to keep learning, I'd much rather help them get going and fill in the gaps along the way.

r001.rationale: The response recommends complementary co-founders, executives, and experienced support teams, but does not recommend peers at similar or slightly more advanced stages of founding.

r002.rationale: The response discusses filling founders’ skill gaps with other people, but does not describe a career-stage shift from building one’s own skills early to hiring others for those skills later.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so at AI Fund, we actually build companies from scratch, and a lot of what we do is pair up with someone who's really strong in some dimension but has a gap somewhere else. And I think the first thing I'd say is that almost everyone has gaps. I've been doing this for a long time and I still have gaps. So the question isn't whether you have them, it's whether you know what they are and whether you can fill them quickly enough.

One pattern we see a lot is a brilliant technical founder, someone who really knows how to build, but who's never had to sell anything or has never managed a team of more than three people. And the mistake is often to think, "Well, I'll figure it out as I go." Sometimes that works. But the pace of a startup is so fast that if you're learning a critical skill on the job from zero, the company can run out of runway before you get good at it.

So what we try to do is a few things. One is just honest diagnosis. We'll sit down with the founder and go through, okay, here are the ten things this business needs to be good at in the next twelve months. Which of these do you already know how to do? Which of these have you done once? Which have you never done? And people are often more honest about this than you'd expect, if you create a safe environment for it.

Then the second thing is deciding, for each gap, do you learn it, do you hire it, or do you partner for it? Not every gap needs to be closed by the founder personally. If you've never done enterprise sales, maybe the right move is to bring in a cofounder or an early hire who has. But some things, like making product decisions, like setting the culture, I think the founder really does have to learn, because you can't delegate those.

And the third thing is just surrounding people with others who've done it before. A lot of what AI Fund does is pretty unglamorous. It's connecting a first-time CEO with someone who's run a sales team, so they can ask the dumb questions in private rather than making an expensive mistake in public. I find that founders learn remarkably fast when they have someone to call who'll just tell them the truth.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking you need to be complete before you start. You don't. The best founders I know were quite incomplete when they started. They were just very fast learners and very good at recognizing what they didn't know.

r001.rationale: The response recommends connecting founders with experienced people who have done the work, but does not recommend peers at similar or slightly more advanced stages of founding.

r002.rationale: It says to learn, hire, or partner to address gaps, but does not describe a shift from developing skills early in a career to hiring for them later.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to make the gaps specific. Saying someone is a first-time founder doesn’t tell you very much. They might be a fantastic engineer who’s never sold anything, or they might understand the customer really well but need help building the product. Those are very different needs.

Then the question is: What should they learn, and where should they get help? You don’t need every founder to become great at everything. Sometimes a little coaching lets them get through a task themselves. Sometimes they need a co-founder or an early hire with a complementary skill set.

I like helping people work through a concrete problem. Let’s talk to a customer together. Let’s look at why this prototype isn’t working. You help the company move forward, but you also give the founder practice making those decisions. The goal is for them to become increasingly capable of doing it independently.

r001.rationale: The response suggests coaching, a co-founder, or an early hire, but does not recommend surrounding founders with peers at similar or more advanced stages.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning skills versus getting help, but does not identify a shift from developing one’s own skills earlier in a career to hiring others later.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the first things is to make the gaps specific. Saying, “I don’t know how to build a company” is overwhelming. Saying, “I don’t know how to interview customers,” or “I haven’t hired an engineer before”—those are things you can work on.

Then the question is whether you should learn that skill, find a co-founder who brings it, or get help from someone who’s done it before. You don’t need to become great at everything. But you do need enough understanding to make good decisions and recognize when you need help.

For a first-time founder, I think having someone work alongside you on a concrete decision can be much more useful than general advice. Let’s look at what you’re building, what you’ve learned from customers, and what you should test next. That helps the company move forward while the founder develops the skills they’re missing.

r001.rationale: The response suggests finding a co-founder or getting help, but does not recommend peers at similar or slightly more advanced founding stages.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning skills or getting help, but does not describe a shift from developing one’s own skills early in a career to hiring others to supply them later.
